lessons.title: Dairy breeds and the lactation cycle
lessons.html:
Dairy farming in South Africa

Dairy farms in South Africa are found mainly in the coastal and higher-rainfall areas such as the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, where pastures grow well. Some farms run cows on irrigated ryegrass and kikuyu pastures; others keep cows in sheds and feed a total mixed ration (TMR).

Common dairy breeds

BreedFeatures
Holstein-FriesianBlack and white; highest milk volume; needs good feeding
JerseySmall, brown; milk high in butterfat and protein; efficient on pasture
AyrshireRed and white; hardy; good on pasture
GuernseyFawn and white; rich, yellow milk

Crossbred cows are also common because they can be hardier and more fertile.

The lactation cycle

A cow only produces milk after she has calved. The aim on most farms is one calf per cow per year.

  1. Calving - lactation starts. The first milk is colostrum.
  2. Early lactation - milk yield rises to a peak at about six to eight weeks. The cow often loses condition because she cannot eat enough to match her milk output.
  3. Re-breeding - the cow should be inseminated or served again within about three months of calving to keep a yearly calving interval.
  4. Mid and late lactation - yield slowly drops while the cow regains condition.
  5. Dry period - milking stops about two months before the next calving so the udder can rest and the cow can prepare for the next calf.

A typical lactation is counted as about 305 days. Good records of calving dates, services and milk yields allow the manager to plan feeding and breeding.

lessons.title: Milking routine and milk hygiene
lessons.html:
A good milking routine

Cows like routine. Milking at the same times every day, by calm people, gives more milk and fewer udder problems. Shouting or hitting cows causes stress, which blocks milk let-down.

Steps at milking

  1. Bring cows in quietly. Do not run them with dogs or a bakkie.
  2. Wash and dry your hands and wear clean gloves.
  3. Strip the first few squirts from each teat into a strip cup and look for clots, watery milk or blood - signs of mastitis.
  4. Pre-dip or clean the teats and dry each one with its own paper towel.
  5. Attach the cluster within about one to two minutes so you use the let-down reflex.
  6. Do not over-milk. Remove the cluster when the flow stops (many parlours have automatic removal).
  7. Post-dip every teat with teat dip to kill bacteria.
  8. Keep cows standing after milking, for example by giving fresh feed, so teat canals close before they lie down.

Mastitis

Mastitis is an infection of the udder and is the most costly disease on many dairies. Signs include a hot, swollen or hard quarter and abnormal milk. Report cases, mark the cow, and treat only as the vet directs. Milk from treated cows must be kept out of the bulk tank for the full withdrawal period on the label.

Milk hygiene

  • Clean the milking machine and pipes after every milking using the correct detergent and hot water routine.
  • Cool milk quickly in the bulk tank to about 4 degrees Celsius.
  • Keep the parlour, yard and tank room clean, and keep chemicals away from milk.
  • Milk is tested for bacteria, somatic cells and antibiotic residues. Contaminated milk can be rejected, and the farm loses the whole load.

lessons.title: Feeding and caring for the dairy herd
lessons.html:
Feeding for milk

A high-producing cow needs a lot of energy, protein and water. Milk is mostly water, so a cow may drink a very large amount every day, especially in summer. Water troughs near the parlour exit must always be full and clean.

  • Pasture - ryegrass, kikuyu and clover pastures are managed in rotation so cows always graze fresh, leafy grass.
  • Concentrates - given in the parlour or in a TMR to supply extra energy and protein.
  • Roughage - silage and hay keep the rumen healthy and the butterfat up.
  • Minerals - especially calcium and phosphorus. Low blood calcium around calving causes milk fever, where the cow goes down and cannot get up. Call the vet immediately.

Rearing calves

  1. Make sure the calf drinks enough colostrum within the first few hours of life. Colostrum gives the calf the antibodies it needs to fight disease.
  2. Dip the navel with iodine.
  3. House calves in clean, dry, draught-free pens.
  4. Feed milk or milk replacer at the same times every day, and offer clean water and calf starter early so the rumen develops.
  5. Wean when the calf is eating enough starter, according to the farm's programme.

Herd health and safety

  • Follow the vaccination and parasite programme from the vet.
  • Trim hooves and check for lameness; lame cows give less milk.
  • Watch for heat signs (standing to be mounted, restlessness, mucus) and record them.
  • Bulls on a dairy are dangerous. Never work alone in a camp with a bull.
  • Wear gloves and eye protection when handling cleaning chemicals and teat dips.

Key points

  • Holstein gives the most volume; Jersey gives rich milk efficiently on pasture.
  • Aim for one calf per cow per year, with a dry period of about two months.
  • A calm, clean milking routine with pre- and post-dip prevents mastitis.
  • Cool milk fast and keep treated milk out of the tank.
  • Calves must get colostrum within the first hours of life.
